study_type.claude: Design Science Research: expert interviews, use-case demonstration, quasi-experiment (ITS + DiD)
study_type.nlm: Design Science Research: expert interviews, quasi-experiment (ITS + DiD)
study_type.value: Mixed methods (design science research: expert interviews, use-case demonstration, ITS/DiD quasi-experiment)
study_type.note: Both describe the same DSR design with qualitative and quasi-experimental evaluation; Other (DSR framework proposal) or Quasi-experiment could also be argued. Claude flags that the abstract, conclusions and limitations describe only expert-based validation.

research_method.claude: DSR: framework designed from literature review; initial validation by semi-structured expert interviews; use-case demonstration (.NET microservice + Angular front-end, 3 change scenarios over 2 sprints); longitudinal quasi-experiment with ITS and DiD, 2 treated teams vs 1 control over 21 weeks
research_method.nlm: DSR; 3 semi-structured interviews with 4 experts; quasi-experiment with ITS and DiD, 2 treated product teams and 1 matched control over 21 weeks (939 total production deployments)
research_method.value: Design Science Research; framework designed from the literature, initially validated through 3 semi-structured interviews with 4 IT experts, demonstrated in a use case (.NET microservice and Angular front-end); evaluation reported as a 21-week longitudinal quasi-experiment with Interrupted Time-Series and Difference-in-Differences (2 treated product teams vs 1 matched control team; weekly aggregation; DORA and SLO outcomes)
research_method.note: Deployment counts omitted: NotebookLM gives 939 total, Claude gives 238/421 (treated) and 247/261 (control), which the full text confirms (1,167 total).

context.claude: Industry; 4 IT experts from medium to multinational companies; demonstration in authors' environment (GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Prometheus/Grafana); quasi-experiment teams described only as 'product teams' (organization, sector, country not reported)
context.nlm: Industry (software-intensive enterprise IT units and digital service providers); 4 experts; 2 treated teams and 1 control team
context.value: industry; 4 IT experts with experience in medium to multinational companies (3 interviews); use-case demonstration on a .NET/Angular microservices stack with GitHub Actions, Docker and Kubernetes; 2 treated product teams and 1 matched control team (organization and sector not reported)
context.note: NotebookLM's 'enterprise IT units and digital service providers' comes from the literature-review section (3.5.1), not the study setting; omitted.

dora_applied.note: DF, LT, CFR and MTTR are the primary outcome measures of the demonstration and quasi-experiment and form Layer 5 of the framework.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported; interviews via Zoom only.

data_window.claude: 21 weeks (6 baseline, 3 adoption, 12 steady state); no calendar dates
data_window.value: 21 weeks (6-week baseline, 3-week adoption, 12-week steady state; calendar dates not stated)
data_window.note: Duration only; phase split given by Claude and confirmed in the text.

cat_productivity.note: NotebookLM tags lead time 'Delivery / Productivity', but it is a delivery metric; no output/throughput productivity measure.

cat_quality.note: Change failure rate, MTTR, error rate, SLO attainment, critical-path test coverage.

cat_satisfaction.note: Borderline: only team-perceived deployment confidence and process clarity (5-point Likert), tagged Satisfaction by both.

cat_activity.note: NotebookLM tags DF and PR review time 'Activity', but these are delivery/collaboration metrics.

cat_delivery.note: Deployment frequency and lead time for changes.

cat_devex.note: Both tag the Likert items 'DevEx', but the DevEx framework is not used.

cat_agile.note: Claude lists canary/SLO gate outcomes (Process/Governance) and prescribed pipeline metrics (pipeline success %, build time, flaky-test rate); NotebookLM identifies no process metric.

cat_survey.note: 5-point Likert ratings of deployment confidence and process clarity; expert interviews.

evidence.quote: This study followed the Design Science Research (DSR) paradigm to design, instantiate, and evaluate an artifact

We conducted a longitudinal, quasi-experimental evaluation with two treated product teams (T1, T2) and one matched control team (C). The study ran for 21 weeks and was segmented into (i) a 6-week baseline period (business-as-usual), (ii) a 3-week adoption period (framework rollout), and (iii) a 12-week steady-state period (framework used routinely).
evidence.loc: PDF p. 27 (6.2.2 Executed Quasi-Experimental Evaluation (ITS + DiD))

evidence.quote: To validate the proposed framework, three interviews were conducted with four experts in the IT industry. All the people interviewed have experience in medium to multinational companies
This section illustrates how the proposed framework can be applied in practice through a realistic end-to-end implementation using a .NET microservice and an Angular front-end.
Deployment Frequency (DORA): count of successful production deployments per unit time, computed from CI/CD deployment job completions
Lead Time for Changes (DORA): time from code change acceptance to production (e.g., PR merge timestamp → production deployment completion timestamp).
Change Failure Rate (DORA): proportion of deployments that result in service impairment requiring rollback, hotfix, or incident creation.
SLO attainment (p95 Latency < 250 ms; error rate < 1%): improved from 96.1% to 99.2% weekly compliance; error-budget burn rate decreased 58%.
Critical-path test coverage: +18 pp (from 62% → 80%). PR review time: −23% median. Deployment confidence (5-point Likert): +1.1 points; process clarity: +0.9 points.
